results.summary: GRE and SWI sequences sensitively detect hemosiderin deposition in cavernous malformations and occult vascular lesions, with blooming artifact exceeding lesion size on conventional sequences. output.summary: Cavernous malformations are a recognized structural cause of lesional focal epilepsy, responsible for 5-10% of temporal lobe epilepsy cases. First-line AED options for focal epilepsy in women of childbearing age include lamotrigine and levetiracetam. Earlier surgical intervention is associated with better long-term seizure outcomes.

differential.diagnosis: Hemorrhagic low-grade temporal neoplasm (e.g., ganglioglioma with hemorrhage)
differential.key_features: MRI can show hemorrhagic signal in low-grade tumors; distinguished from cavernoma by absence of enhancement, presence of solid enhancement, and growth on follow-up imaging — classic cavernoma morphology (popcorn + hemosiderin rim + no edema) on epilepsy-protocol MRI with GRE/SWI blooming argues strongly against.

differential.diagnosis: Focal epilepsy secondary to hippocampal sclerosis (mesial temporal sclerosis)
differential.key_features: Normal bilateral hippocampal volumes and normal T2/FLAIR signal on epilepsy-protocol MRI; cavernoma is the concordant lesion.

differential.diagnosis: Cavernous malformation presenting as acute hemorrhage (mimicking stroke)
differential.key_features: Absence of acute restricted diffusion or perilesional edema, chronic hemosiderin ring, and stereotyped recurrent focal seizures over months distinguish chronic epileptogenic cavernoma from acute hemorrhage.

differential.diagnosis: Focal cortical dysplasia (type II) of right temporal lobe
differential.key_features: FCD typically shows transmantle sign, blurring of gray-white junction, and FLAIR cortical signal on epilepsy-protocol MRI; no such features identified; discrete cavernoma accounts for findings.
Video-EEG captures two habitual events with right anterior temporal electrographic correlate; structural cavernoma concordant with seizure focus.

key_clinical_evidence: The outside report of a 'possible prior small hemorrhage' is the red herring: the characteristic GRE/SWI blooming far exceeding lesion size, complete hemosiderin rim, popcorn mixed signal, and absence of perilesional edema or enhancement identify this as a chronic cavernous malformation, not an acute or subacute vascular event.

Laterality is self-consistent: right temporal cavernoma produces right anterior temporal EEG sharps, right-hemispheric seizure onset, and LEFT-sided hand automatisms and head version — correctly indicating right hemisphere, non-dominant (left-handed patient, right hemisphere may be language-dominant, but visuospatial functions are right-lateralized).

GRE and SWI sequences are essential components of the epilepsy MRI protocol for any patient with suspected lesional epilepsy; absence of these sequences risks missing the cavernoma or misclassifying it as a non-vascular lesion.
Cavernous malformations are the cause of approximately 5-10% of lesional focal temporal epilepsy; surgical resection offers 70-80% seizure freedom in well-selected patients.
The elevated prolactin drawn two hours post-event provides limited interpretive value (optimal draw is within 10-20 minutes); do not base diagnostic conclusions on it.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.

July 2026 review applied end to end: routine EEG first when appropriate, staged sleep-deprived/ambulatory escalation, video only for event capture or tertiary evaluation, and continuous ICU EEG only for NCSE.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Chen is a 38-year-old left-handed East Asian software engineer who presents to the epilepsy monitoring unit for evaluation of recurrent stereotyped spells that have occurred approximately weekly over the past three months. She has no prior history of seizures or neurological illness.

The patient reports that the episodes begin abruptly without clear warning, though on two occasions she noticed a brief sensation of unusual fullness or pressure in her right ear followed by a rising feeling of anxiety immediately before the event. She has no memory of the episodes themselves. Her husband has witnessed two events. He describes her suddenly stopping mid-conversation and staring blankly, then beginning repetitive chewing and swallowing motions. During the most recent episode three days ago, she fumbled with nearby objects with her left hand for approximately 45 to 60 seconds. On one occasion, her head turned slowly to the left. After the episode ended, she appeared confused and disoriented for approximately five minutes before returning to her baseline. She was fatigued for several hours afterward.

The episodes do not involve falls, urinary incontinence, or tongue biting. She denies any preceding headache, visual changes, palpitations, or lightheadedness. She has no history of migraines. There is no history of febrile illness, recent travel, or systemic symptoms. She has not started or changed any medications recently. She is not pregnant.

She was seen two weeks ago by an outside neurologist who ordered a standard MRI brain without epilepsy protocol. The radiologist's report noted a 'small focus of T2 signal and possible prior small hemorrhage in the right temporal lobe' and recommended clinical correlation, but the clinical significance was not further characterized at that visit. The patient was referred for inpatient evaluation at our center.

neurological_exam.additional: No postictal deficits identified at the time of examination, approximately four hours after the most recent episode. Husband describes witnessed events as brief behavioral arrest with mouth-chewing and fumbling movements of the left hand, followed by a period of confusion lasting several minutes. Head version to the left was observed during one episode.
